en: Preface composed by the Śramaṇa Ji of the Great Ci’en Monastery.
Chapter One. I have heard that the Supreme Enlightened One, through his provisional and ultimate teachings, manifested his traces in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings;

that the wondrous pivot of his spirit excels in responding to the multitudes of creatures to raise up the fishing pole [of the Dharma]; and that he shook Mount Rucaka to bring splendor to the great trichiliocosm. As these words soared forth—

He pours forth across the ocean to reach the eighty thousand worlds; like a gathering cloud of compassion, he provides vast protection, and like a sudden downpour of Dharma rain, he brings distant clarity. He nourishes the distinct blossoming of the two types of trees and moistens the diverse luxuriance of the three kinds of grasses.
Yet, because the young merchant grew weary of the long and perilous journey, he was first led and enticed toward the City of Transformation;
and because the young child found delight in the ox-cart, he ultimately attained illumination through the Great Vehicle.

Thus, the Holy Sovereign who vanquished the ten armies untied the great pearl from her topknot; as the King of Physicians who established the Eight Truths, she bestowed the wondrous medicine held in her palm. She adorned the surface of all conventional means (*upāya*) and transcended the boundaries of the hundred schools; she encompassed the seven stages while standing alone in glory amidst the nine divisions, crowning the five vehicles and emerging uniquely preeminent throughout the ages.
How great it is!

It proclaims the single reality and encompasses the vast void; it wields the two powers and leaves behind the net of myriad phenomena. How could the ocean’s bounty be used to compare with its profound intent, or Mount Sumeru its loftiness to match its exalted path?
The title "Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra" at the beginning is the ultimate proclamation that adorns the grand framework, serving as the comprehensive name for the entire work.
The designation "Chapter One: Introduction" is the magnificent standard that mirrors the categories of meaning, revealing the specific title of this distinct vessel.
The Dharma contains and sustains the norms, binding together all auspicious signs to manifest its wondrousness;
the flower, possessing both elegance and brilliance, unites all beauties to reveal the lotus.

Both essence and function are presented, and both the dharma and the metaphor are raised together; the paths of the Half and the Full have already been clarified, and the routes of what to adopt and what to reject are now clearly established.

The Sūtras are the eternal and the Dharma; they are that which gathers and that which penetrates. As the eternal, they serve as the guiding model for a hundred kings; as the Dharma, they provide the pattern for virtue across a thousand generations. "Gathering" means to collect these wondrous principles; "penetrating" means to guide those ordinary beings, so that all may ultimately leave the ford of suffering behind and finally ascend to the shore of enlightenment.

"Preface" (*xu*) means "source" (*you*) and "beginning" (*shi*); it sets forth the causes and conditions from which the teaching arises and the gradual inception through which the Dharma is established.
"Chapter" (*pin*) means "category" (*lei*) and "distinction" (*bie*); it classifies the profound purport into distinct types and categorizes the subtle means by dividing them into streams.
"First" (di) means "subsequent" and "position.
"One" (yi) means "extreme" and "foremost.
This scripture contains twenty-eight categories that systematically organize the True Doctrine; as this chapter follows and occupies the foremost position, it is therefore named "The First."
Regarding the sūtra’s opening, “Thus have I heard,” the commentary states:
First, in explaining the scriptural text, it shall be briefly analyzed by means of six sections.

First, an account of the intent for the arising of the sūtra; second, an elucidation of the sūtra’s central theme; third, an explanation of how the chapters of the sūtra derive their names; fourth, a clarification of the establishment and abolition of the chapters; fifth, a demonstration of the sequence of the chapters; and sixth, an interpretation of the main text of the sūtra.
Regarding the first point, the purpose for which this sutra was composed, it can be briefly summarized by five meanings:

first, to respond to requests; second, to refute doubts and attachments; third, to manifest the records and practices; fourth, to benefit future generations; and fifth, to reveal the timing and circumstances.
In responding to the inquiry regarding causes, there are two parts:
first, responding to the causes; second, responding to the request.
Regarding the initial response to the causes, there are six points:

First, repaying the cause of practice; second, repaying the cause of aspiration; third, repaying the cause of seeking; fourth, repaying the cause of upholding; fifth, repaying the cause of characteristics; sixth, repaying the cause of exposition.
The fruit of Buddhahood cannot be achieved in vain; it must be attained through karmic practice. Practice does not arise in isolation; it must be sustained by aspiration.

Although practice and aspiration may arise spontaneously, they cannot converge alone without conditions. Even when meeting with conditions to seek further weightiness, the fruit is not accomplished through mere impulsiveness. One must rely on upholding the teachings and study before the fruit can be attained. Once the attainment of the fruit is perfected, one will manifest in response to sentient beings.

To manifest the profound and subtle essence of the sūtra’s central tenet, it first reveals the causes for the appearance of the Great Signs; since these signs have been made manifest, their underlying principles must be expounded. Therefore, it is designated that the Buddha’s original advent into the world was for the sake of this one great matter.
By means of this, the causes are requited through these six meanings.

Regarding the requital of the cause of practice, the *Upāya-paryāya* (Chapter on Expedient Means) explains the eight kinds of profundity according to the treatise’s commentary on the sutra as follows:

"The Buddha has personally attended upon countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas; he has fully practiced the immeasurable path-dharmas of all Buddhas; his courageous diligence is universally renowned; he has accomplished profound and unprecedented dharmas; that which is difficult to understand, the Tathāgata alone can know; the underlying intent of what he teaches according to suitability is difficult to understand, and cannot be known by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."

Regarding the eight kinds of profundity: first, the profundity of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting; second, the profundity of practice; third, the profundity of the conduct of fruition; fourth, the profundity of the mind that increases merit; fifth, the profundity of the mind of sublime excellence; sixth, the unsurpassed; seventh, the entry; and eighth, the profundity of the non-common maintenance and sustaining of what is performed by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The sutra contains only six [perfections], lacking the sixth and the eighth; this shall be understood later.

Since the Buddha-way and its teachings have been fully practiced, and only by fully cultivating the causes of the One Vehicle’s seed-wisdom does one attain the fruit of Buddhahood, the present teaching of this wondrous Dharma in response to those causes exhorts the cultivation of causal practices.
Regarding the cause of fulfilling vows, the "Expedient Means" chapter states:
"Listen well, Śāriputra!
I originally established a vow, desiring to cause all sentient beings to be no different from myself."
"As my original vow, which I made in the past, has now been fulfilled; I shall transform all sentient beings and cause them to enter the Buddha-way.
The "Chapter on the Lifespan" states:
"I constantly have this thought: 'By what means can I cause sentient beings to enter the Buddha-way and swiftly achieve the Buddha-body?'"

Whether in former causal stages or in the present state of fruition, he has always made the vow that all sentient beings, like his own body, might enter the Buddha-way; therefore, to fulfill this original vow, he preaches this sutra.
Furthermore, it is so that sentient beings may also give rise to this vow, for when practice and vow correspond, one attains transcendence from the world.
Regarding the cause for seeking [the Dharma], the "Devadatta Chapter" states:
"In the past, I sought the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* without weariness; throughout many kalpas, I constantly served as a king, seeking great bodhi without ever turning back."
He beat the drum and issued a proclamation to the four quarters, at which time a seer came and addressed the king, saying:
"I possess a Mahāyāna sūtra titled 'The Lotus Sutra of the Sublime Dharma. If you do not go back on your word to me, I shall proclaim it for you."

Upon hearing the words of the rishi, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He immediately followed the rishi, providing all that was required; even using his own body as a bed and seat, he never grew weary in body or mind. He served the rishi for a thousand years, ensuring that nothing was lacking for the sake of seeking the Dharma.
"The king of that time was my present self; the seer of that time was Devadatta.

Thus, although the Buddha’s past vows and practices have been fulfilled, they necessarily depend upon the convergence of conditions; he always held this sutra in high regard and devoted himself exclusively to seeking it from virtuous friends.
Therefore, I now proclaim this so that a desire for the profound may arise.

Regarding the cause for upholding [this teaching], among the eight types of profundity mentioned previously, the first is that the Buddha himself once attended upon countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, whereupon he received, upheld, read, and recited the profound [Dharma].

The first stage of reliance involves a bodhisattva making offerings to five *gaṅgā*-sands of Buddhas; the second stage of reliance involves a bodhisattva making offerings to six *gaṅgā*-sands of Buddhas; the third stage of reliance involves a bodhisattva making offerings to seven *gaṅgā*-sands of Buddhas; and the fourth stage of reliance involves a bodhisattva making offerings to eight *gaṅgā*-sands of Buddhas, encountering many virtuous friends and upholding [the teachings] for a long duration.

Furthermore, in the past, when Śākyamuni Tathāgata was himself the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, he practiced the conduct of Never-Disparaging after the parinirvāṇa of Buddha King of Majestic Sound. At the time of his death, he heard twenty quadrillion verses of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* being recited in the void, and he was able to receive and uphold them all.
He immediately attained the aforementioned purity of the six sense faculties and further increased his lifespan by two hundred trillion nayutas of years, extensively expounding this sutra.
After the end of his life, he encountered two thousand koṭis of Buddhas, all named Candrasūryapradīpa, and constantly upheld this sutra under them.

For these reasons, he further encountered two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, all equally named Cloud Sovereign Lamp King (*Meghasvararāja*), under whose teachings he likewise upheld this sutra and constantly attained the aforementioned purity of the six sense faculties. That "Never-Disparaging" one was none other than myself; therefore, because he constantly upheld this sutra in the past, I now speak of it to exhort you to always uphold it.

Regarding the "retribution of mutual causality": having already attained Buddhahood and being about to preach this sutra, he first preached the *Anantārthasūtra* for the bodhisattvas, and subsequently entered the *Anantārthavihārasamādhi*.

Heaven rained down four kinds of flowers and the earth shook in six ways; the fourfold assembly gazed up in reverence and the eight classes of beings rejoiced. He emitted magnificent rays of light that reached afar, and when the multitude saw this, doubt arose within them.
Maitreya posed the question, and Mañjuśrī replied:

"As I contemplate it, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, now intends to proclaim the Great Dharma; he shall rain down the great rain of Dharma, blow the great conch shell of Dharma, beat the great drum of Dharma, and expound the great meaning of Dharma."
In the past, I have witnessed this very omen: after emitting such light, the Tathāgata would immediately preach the Great Dharma, as has been extensively described.
Today, the Tathāgata shall preach a Mahāyāna sūtra titled "The Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma."

"When the Buddhas of the three periods of time are about to preach this sutra, they must first manifest these various great signs; this is not the case with other sutras, for other sutras lack such initial great signs."
Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, this must be explained; thus, prior to expounding this sutra, a great sign (*mahānimitta*) was first manifested.
The manifestation of this great sign was for the purpose of expounding this sutra.
Regarding the explanation of the cause, it says below: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal matter," and so forth, as explained at length.
"There are no śrāvaka disciples; I teach only bodhisattvas, ultimately enabling them to attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).

Therefore, when the Buddhas of the three periods of time achieve ultimate enlightenment, they invariably preach the One Vehicle (ekayāna); these are all skillful means (upāya) employed during the causal stage to lead beings toward the goal.

Although my cultivation and study were complete, I never before expounded [this teaching]; yet now, as the opportunity has arrived, it must not be left unfulfilled. Therefore, following the causes of past lives, I shall speak this wondrous Dharma.
The preceding categories of meaning and scriptural passages are very numerous; fearing that the reader might become weary by their prolixity, I have provided only a brief indication and description.

Regarding the subsequent fulfillment of the request, it is as stated in the sūtras: immediately upon birth, the Bodhisattva took seven steps, emitting a great radiance that illuminated the ten directions. Looking around in all four directions, he let out a lion’s roar and spoke these verses:
"My births from a womb are ended; this is my very last body. I have attained liberation, and I shall now deliver sentient beings."
Having made this vow, his body gradually grew, and as he went out through the four gates, he beheld an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and the appearance of a śramaṇa.
Having questioned those who recognized them, he desired to abandon his kinsmen and seek the unsurpassed fruit.

Observing during the middle watch of the night, he saw that the musicians, queens, and court ladies appeared like stinking corpses, deeply loathsome. He immediately commanded Chandaka to saddle Kanthaka; with the devas supporting his feet, he departed from the city at midnight. Traveling fourteen yojanas, he reached the forest where the seer Bhārgava resided. There, he shaved his hair with a sword, traded his exquisite jeweled robes for a deerskin garment, and sent Chandaka back to inform the royal father.

On the banks of the Nairañjanā River, at the place where the six heretical teachers resided, he practiced asceticism for six years in order to subdue them; his diligent suffering exceeded theirs, as he consumed only hemp and wheat daily until, weary of their heterodox path, he finally partook of the milk-rice gruel.

Having received the auspicious *kuśa* grass, he proceeded to the Bodhi tree and sat upon the Vajrāsana; through the power of wisdom, he subdued the armies of Māra and realized Great Enlightenment, forever transcending the three realms.

At that time, the Lord of the Trichiliocosm and other devas came to the Buddha’s presence and requested him to turn the wheel of Dharma. The transformation Buddhas praised them and exhorted them to teach expediently, for the time was not yet ripe; they were to teach through skillful means and had not yet spoken the ultimate truth.

Now that the occasion is appropriate, Śāriputra and others requested an exposition on the provisional and ultimate realms of the vehicles; Mañjuśrī and others requested an exposition on the practices for peace and bliss of the vehicles; and Maitreya and others requested an exposition on the fruits of the true and emanation bodies.
Therefore, the subsequent scripture says:
"When I first sat at the site of enlightenment, I gazed upon the tree and also practiced walking meditation; for three periods of seven days, I constantly contemplated this matter."
Reflecting further upon the skillful means employed by the Buddhas of the past, [I thought: "The path I have now attained should likewise be taught as the three vehicles.
While I was engaged in this reflection, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared and comforted me with Brahma-sounds, saying:
"Excellent, Śākyamuni!"
"Following all Buddhas, he employs the power of skillful means.
It was for this reason that he provisionally taught the Three Vehicles.
Now that the capacities of beings have matured, Śāriputra and others have requested him to expound the True Doctrine and reveal this Single Reality.
Therefore, the subsequent scripture states:
"Since you have earnestly made this request three times, how could I now refrain from speaking?
In the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices," Mañjuśrī offers his request, and the World-Honored One extensively expounds the four peaceful practices.
In the "Chapter on the Lifespan" it is likewise so: after Maitreya had requested three times, the Buddha said, "You all should believe and understand the Tathāgata’s words of truth."
After exhorting them to have faith three times, he then spoke of the true and the responsive aspects of the body; thus, in response to their request, he preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Within the section on destroying doubt and attachment, there are two parts:
first, destroying doubt; second, destroying attachment.

Regarding the "Dispelling of Doubts": After the Buddha had attained enlightenment himself, he recorded only that bodhisattvas would attain bodhi, and did not state that śrāvakas could attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

Because śrāvakas and others harbored doubts that they would never become Buddhas, Śāriputra was deeply moved by his own loss of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision, as explained at length in the sūtra.

Now, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented and marvelous Dharma never heard before, all our doubts and regrets have been severed. Previously, when the various lesser bodhisattvas heard of the Mahāyāna, they also doubted that the Bodhi of enlightenment was attained by bodhisattvas alone and that śrāvakas had no share in it; or else, those lesser bodhisattvas of indeterminate nature doubted that they themselves had no share in the Buddha’s Bodhi.
Consequently, all three vehicles possess a net of doubt.
As this sutra states:
"Whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, upon hearing the Dharma I have taught—even so much as a single verse—they shall all undoubtedly attain Buddhahood."
It further states:
"For all those seeking the three vehicles who may have doubts or regrets, the Buddha shall eliminate and sever them for them, so that they are exhausted without remainder.
It also says:
"When the Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed; the twelve hundred Arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas.

Herein, the destruction of doubt also simultaneously destroys regret. Previously, they regretted practicing the Lesser Vehicle and failing to become Buddhas; now, hearing that they can indeed become Buddhas, the reason for their regret is eliminated, as they realize that the Lesser Vehicle is actually the cause for the Great Vehicle.

Doubt pertains to all three vehicles, whereas regret belongs only to the Śrāvaka vehicle; since the broad encompasses the narrow, it is said that one "destroys doubt" rather than "removes regret. The distinction between these shall be explained later in this volume; therefore, this wondrous Dharma is taught for the purpose of destroying doubt.
Regarding the subsequent refutation of those who cling [to the view of the śrāvaka], there are two types of śrāvakas:
first, those of determinate lineage, who, having attained the fruit of a śrāvaka, will certainly enter the nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa where the body is reduced to ashes and wisdom is extinguished.
Therefore, various sūtras state:
"The roots of goodness of other persons are exhausted at the time of nirvāṇa, but the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva are not so.

Regarding those who have twice regressed and subsequently again generated the mind for great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*): the former are of fixed lineage (*niyata-gotra*), while the latter are of unfixed lineage (*aniyata-gotra*).
However, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Dharmapada-sūtra-śāstra* state that there are four types of śrāvakas:
first, those of the determined lineage, also called "those who incline toward tranquility";
second, those of overweening pride, who are ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) that have attained the fourth dhyāna and claim to be arhats.
Those who have three times regressed and yet again give rise to the mind of great bodhicitta are also called those of indeterminate lineage.

For instance, those śrāvakas who received predictions at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are termed "those who have regressed from bodhicitta"; Śāriputra and others are all of this class. Thus, the sūtra itself says:
"Addressing Śāriputra:"
"In the past, I taught you to aspire to the Buddha-way, yet now you have forgotten it all and instead claim that you have already attained nirvana.
The *Upāsaka-sūtra* states:

"Śāriputra cultivated the Mahāyāna path for sixty kalpas; however, because he gave away his eyes, his great practice was difficult to complete, and he regressed to seek the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle."
Śāriputra also stated that he had already received transformation through the Buddha in life after life.

The "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter explains the beginning of the karmic connection established in the past by the sixteen princes when they transformed sentient beings; for this reason, it is said that one may "retrogress from the bodhicitta. This does not mean that all those of indeterminate lineage are of the class who retrogress; there are also those who previously did not seek the Great [Vehicle], but now proceed toward the Great from the small fruits, precisely because they are of indeterminate lineage.
Fourth is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); such a transformation body is not the ultimate reality.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The great bodhisattvas and Buddhas manifest transformations appearing as śrāvakas in order to lead actual śrāvakas toward the Mahāyāna; Pūrṇa and others are examples of this class."
The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states:
"In this context, predictions are given only to two types of śrāvakas: those who have regressed from their resolve and those who are transformation-bodies (nirmāṇakāya).
As for those who have entered quiescence and those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), the Buddha does not grant them predictions because their faculties are not yet mature."
Although the Bodhisattva’s bestowal of a prophecy is stated in general terms—
“You shall practice the bodhisattva path and attain Buddhahood”—

the treatise explains that this prophecy is given to inspire the arousal of the mind. It is precisely for those whose roots of virtue have matured but who have regressed from the bodhicitta that the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is taught, in order to correctly shatter their attachments.
The manifested transformation is not the ultimate reality; since there is no attachment to be refuted, it is permissible to display such signs.
Because those of overweening pride are ordinary beings whose faculties have neither yet matured nor manifested, the Buddha does not grant them a prediction of enlightenment.

Regarding the Bodhisattva who bestows predictions: this refers to the case of Nityapradīpa (Always-Not-Light), who served as the causal basis for the prediction; he was led to believe that he possessed the lineage of a Buddha, and furthermore, he gradually gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and cultivated the Great Practice.
Since those who have entered the state of tranquility (śamaikāyana) lack the lineage of the Mahāyāna, how can one discuss whether they are mature or immature?
One should say that because those who have entered tranquility lack the Mahāyāna lineage, their faculties are not matured, and thus the Buddha does not grant them a prediction [of enlightenment].

A Bodhisattva bestows a prediction (vyākaraṇa) based on the complete presence of the causal factors of lineage and principle, gradually causing [the individual] to believe in the Mahāyāna because they are not deluded regarding the Dharma.

This is not the case for those whose faculties are not yet matured, though they may become mature later; therefore, it is not a prediction bestowed by a Bodhisattva that causes one to set out with the mind of the Mahāyāna, declaring, "You shall become a Buddha."

The Bodhisattva’s aspirational mind employs skillful means to transform beings and cause them to give rise to faith; as stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, "I shall lead all to enter nirvana without remainder, yet not all have entered final extinction," the Bodhisattva’s prediction regarding their progression toward tranquility is likewise so.

If one were to concede that those who have entered quiescence (śamaikāyana) are identical to those with overweening pride (adhimāna), then not only would they fail to be called "those who have entered quiescence," but this would also severely contradict various scriptures, as the meanings would be incompatible.

This is because those who have entered quiescence and those with overweening pride are spoken of together in one place; the primary translators likewise stated that their faculties were immature and thus they were made to resolve their minds [on enlightenment]. However, the correct meaning should be: because the faculties of those who have entered quiescence were immature, the Buddha did not grant them a prediction (vyākaraṇa);

whereas for Bodhisattvas, he granted predictions so as to cause them to develop faith and resolve toward the Mahāyāna. For those with overweening pride, because their faculties were immature, the Buddha did not grant a prediction; whereas for Bodhisattvas, he granted predictions so as to cause them to develop the mind directed toward the Mahāyāna.
If those who have entered the state of tranquility were later to also become Buddhas, it would contradict the scriptural passages found throughout the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other texts.
Bodhisattvas are also of two types:
first, those of sudden enlightenment; second, those of gradual enlightenment.
Gradual enlightenment has two meanings:

first, if one awakens the mind and turns toward the Great [Vehicle] after having attained the fruits of the Two Vehicles, this is termed gradual enlightenment, because the number of births remaining is small or non-existent altogether.

If one returns from the two types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to the Great Vehicle, this is subsumed under sudden enlightenment (*tongwu*), because they have never yet realized the fruits of the Two Vehicles.

Since their remaining births are still numerous, this is not called gradual enlightenment (*jianwu*); therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks only of eighty thousand kalpas for the noble ones (*ārya*), but does not mention the number of kalpas for ordinary beings (*i-sheng*) who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna].

Second, those who merely follow from having previously aroused the two minds and previously cultivated the two practices, and subsequently return to the Great [Vehicle], are all termed "gradual enlighteners.

Because they possess that lineage and because they have cultivated those practices, their understanding through hearing and reflection is also called "enlightenment"—why must it necessarily be realized enlightenment?

Furthermore, there are also those with a small number of births remaining—namely, those for whom birth is already determined, such as at the very moment of this birth, or those who have attained the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) while seated.
Since the Sūtra bases its reckoning on kalpas and speaks only of noble ones (*ārya*), what prevents ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) from having a small number of births remaining?

Regarding the principle of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) taught in this sutra, although the treatise states that it was spoken for two types of śrāvakas—namely, those who have regressed from their resolve and those who are transformational beings—the single assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is primarily intended for those who have regressed from the bodhicitta, while also including transformational beings, as evidenced by the presence of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra and others within the assembly.

If one follows the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) should be explained by means of ten principles; yet, there is no logical error in treating these principles as three, for those of the determined lineage (*niyata-gotra*) are not deluded regarding the Dharma, those of the undetermined lineage (*aniyata-gotra*) turn toward the Great [Vehicle], and those who are emanations (*nirmāṇa*) do so for the sake of transforming others through their predictions (*vyākaraṇa*).
Although this may also be spoken for the sake of the two types of bodhisattvas, the main teaching is intended solely for those of gradual enlightenment.
Therefore, the scripture below states:
"When bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed. In meaning, this also encompasses sudden enlightenment; thus, it does not deviate from the underlying principle.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains the ten meanings of the One Vehicle as follows:
"In order to attract and gather one class of beings, and to sustain the remainder, the Buddhas teach the One Vehicle on account of those with indeterminate lineage."
This refers to a certain class of śrāvakas who have been drawn away from the bodhicitta and have regressed from it;
as well as those other gradual-awakening bodhisattvas and śrāvakas who have regressed from the bodhicitta because they cling to the lesser fruits, considering them to be ultimate.
Śāriputra said:
"I have completely eliminated all false views and attained realization of the dharma of emptiness; at that time, my mind thought to itself that I had reached nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa also said:
"The Buddha has caused us to emerge from the triple world and attain the realization of nirvana, yet we have not given rise to even a single thought of delight toward the Dharma of the bodhisattvas.
All of this is due to our past attachment to the narrow-mindedness of the śrāvaka vehicle."
As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The three types of refining the mind eliminate the obstacles in four areas, taking the Dharma and its meaning as objects.
Regarding these "four areas":

First, mental attention directed toward the [lower] vehicles; second, the state of being free from doubt regarding various doubts; third, regarding the teachings one has heard and contemplated, claiming "I am capable of this while others cannot"; and fourth, attachment to conceptualization, ranging from the skeleton up to enlightenment.

Regarding the mental engagement of those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), because they cling to their respective fruits as being ultimate, this sutra was taught to sever such clinging. Furthermore, for bodhisattvas who awaken gradually (*anupūrvābhisambodhi*) and who, clinging to the thought that Buddha-enlightenment (*buddhabodhi*) is not their portion, wish to fall back and remain within the two vehicles, this [sutra] was taught to sustain them so that they do not regress.

Furthermore, there are those bodhisattvas of limited capacity who have attained sudden awakening, yet cling to the notion that Buddhahood can only be attained by practicing based on the Mahāyāna, while those already established as śrāvakas cannot become Buddhas.
Now, this misconception is refuted to demonstrate that the Two Vehicles are not ultimate and that those abiding in the Two Vehicles can also attain Buddhahood;

therefore, this sutra is preached. Consequently, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* eliminates four points of doubt: first, the mental orientation of the Two Vehicles; second, the thought "I am capable [of this], whereas others are not. These two types of doubts being removed are precisely what was mentioned previously.
The section on manifesting the prediction and the practice has two parts:
first, manifesting the prediction; second, manifesting the practice.

Regarding the first, manifesting the prediction: since the Buddha attained enlightenment himself, he had not yet conferred the prediction of bodhi upon the śrāvakas; it is for the purpose of conferring such predictions now that he preaches this sutra.
Therefore, the subsequent sutra says:
"I have established these skillful means to enable you to enter the Buddha-wisdom; I have never said to you that you shall attain the path of the Buddha."
The reason I have not yet spoken is that the time for speaking had not yet arrived;
now is precisely the right time, and I shall definitively expound the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa said:

Furthermore, we are now already advanced in years; regarding the Buddha’s teaching on the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for bodhisattvas, we have not produced even a single thought of joy or aspiration. Yet, hearing before the Buddha today that we, as śrāvakas, are to receive the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, our hearts are filled with a joy such as we have never experienced before.
It further says:
"Some speak of the Sūtras, Gāthās, Itivṛttakas, Jātakas, and Adbhutadharmas;
they also speak of the Nidānas, Avadānas, along with the Geyas and Upadeśa-sūtras."

"Previously, for the sake of the śrāvakas alone, these nine divisions [of the scriptures] were taught, but the vyākaraṇa (prophecies), vaipulya (extensive teachings), and udāna (inspired utterances) were not taught; therefore, because those were not previously prophesied and are now being prophesied, this sūtra is spoken."

Regarding the subsequent manifestation of practice: what is now being taught is the bodhisattva’s practice of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), for the One Vehicle is precisely the practice of the bodhisattva.
Therefore, the sutra below states:

"There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure, who are gentle and of sharp faculties; having been in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, they have practiced the profound and wondrous path. For these sons of the Buddha, I preach this Mahāyāna sutra."
It is further said:
"Whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, upon hearing the Dharma I have preached, even so much as a single verse, they shall all undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.
It is also said:
"Śāriputra! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach and transform only bodhisattvas; all that they do is always for the sake of a single purpose.

This requires cultivating merit and wisdom, illuminating both existence and emptiness, following the teachings to express the truth and investigating the profound principle, so that true understanding arises and one awakens to the One Vehicle."

Furthermore, the One Vehicle possesses both cause and fruit. The cause consists of the seven stages and the four practices of the Bodhisattvas; these are all fully assigned below according to their respective requirements.
The fruit consists of the stage of Buddhahood, namely Bodhi and Nirvana.
All of these are fully encompassed within the three bodies (*trikāya*). Furthermore, the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) occurs in three stages:

the *Anlehang pin* (Chapter on Peaceful Practices) and others clarify the realm of the One Vehicle; the *Shouliang pin* (Chapter on the Lifespan) and others clarify the fruit of the One Vehicle. Clarifying the realm is intended to inspire the aspiration for the Śrāvaka mind, while clarifying the practice is to cause one to cultivate the Bodhisattva path; it is through this that one ultimately anticipates the merit of the Buddha-fruit. Therefore, in order to manifest the Bodhisattva practices, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was preached.
There are two types of benefit for the present:
first, benefit for the present; second, benefit for the future.

Regarding the first, benefit for the present: all ordinary beings and sages present at the single assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are suitable to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and thereby gain benefit. This consists of two categories:
First is the benefit of the prediction of the fruit; second is the benefit of present realization.

Regarding the benefit of the prediction of the fruit: for the sake of the three types of capacities, the World-Honored One expounded the meaning of the One Vehicle in three cycles, harmonizing the two [vehicles] and subverting the two [views] to benefit those of the present.

From the "Expedient Means" chapter down to the "Parable" chapter, following the section where Śāriputra receives his prediction and the eight classes of beings express their joy and praise, this constitutes the first cycle.
The Sūtra states:

"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition; even so, through the power of expedient means, the Buddhas differentiate and teach the three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle."

Thus, having heard these words, Śāriputra gained deep understanding and realization within the "Parable Chapter"; after the Buddha confirmed his realization, he was granted a prediction of enlightenment.

The "Parable Chapter" (Upamā-parivarta), in which Śāriputra requests the Buddha to preach parables, along with the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (Adhimukti-parivarta), the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" (Oṣadhī-parivarta), and the "Chapter on Prophecy" (Vyākaraṇa-parivarta) constitute the second turning.
The "Parable Chapter" states:

"The Tathāgata is likewise so; he is the father of all sentient beings... Śāriputra, by this cause and condition you should know that it is through the power of the skillful means of the Buddhas that they distinguish and preach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle."

After Mahākāśyapa and the others heard this teaching, they finally attained realization within the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding. The Buddha further confirmed and perfected their understanding in the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs," and in the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions," he bestowed predictions upon the four individuals: Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana.

The "Parable of the City of Illusion" chapter, the "Chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples," and the "Chapter on the Prophecy for Those in Training and Those Beyond Training" constitute the third cycle.
In the "Parable of the City of Illusion" chapter, the Buddha first recounts the deeds of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū to cause [the assembly] to remember them, and further says: "O Bhikṣus!

When the Tathāgata knows for himself that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived... this is merely the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-vidhi*), whereby he distinguishes and teaches three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle."

Having heard this teaching, Pūrṇa and the others gained profound understanding within the "Chapter on the Prophecy to the Five Hundred Disciples. After the Buddha confirmed their realization, he bestowed prophecies upon the five hundred disciples as well as those who were learners and non-learners; this was for the benefit of the present assembly of śrāvakas.
The Sūtra sets forth six modes of manifestation for the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*):
first, the individual prediction, which is given to Śāriputra and the four great śrāvaka disciples because their names and titles differ.
Second is simultaneous prediction (*sahābhisambodhana*), because five hundred people such as Pūrṇa and twelve hundred others share the same name, they are all predicted at the same time.

Third is subsequent prediction (*paścād-abhisambodhana*); those who are neither learners (*śaikṣa*) nor those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), and who are not widely known to the assembly, share a common title and are predicted at a later time among those of inferior faculties.
Fourth is the prediction without enmity, which demonstrates that the Tathāgata is free from resentment and malice; thus, he grants a prediction to Devadatta.

Fifth is the prediction of universal practice, which reveals that women—whether lay or ordained—attain the fruit of Buddhahood by cultivating the bodhisattva path; thus, he grants predictions to the bhikṣuṇīs and the goddesses.
The aforementioned five types of predictions all concern the benefits of the present time and are the Tathāgata’s predictions.

Sixth is the prediction based on the fulfillment of causes: the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging prostrated and praised others, saying, "I do not disparage you; you shall all become Buddhas. Because this demonstrates that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, this single type of prediction given by a bodhisattva is said to concern the benefits of the past.
The first three and the fifth [categories of] benefit derive from hearing the *Lotus Sūtra* prophecy; the remaining two types do not arise from hearing this prophecy.
Nevertheless, these first five prophecies are all termed "benefit in the present," which refers specifically to the benefit of the prophecy regarding the fruit.
However, regarding the transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) received by the śrāvakas after their prediction, the characteristics, essence, and meaning thereof shall be understood later.

As for those who have realized benefit in the present, there are many types; for instance, although the emergence from the dragon palace and the attainment of the Way by the dragon girl—as described in the "Devadatta Chapter"—were both due to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they were not benefits conferred during the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, and thus are omitted here.

Only when the dragon girl attained the Way and preached the Dharma did the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, the eight classes of gods, dragons, and others—both human and non-human—of the Sahā world all see from afar that dragon girl become a Buddha, universally preaching the Dharma for the assembly of gods and humans; their hearts were filled with great joy, and they all paid homage from afar.

Innumerable sentient beings heard the Dharma and attained realization, reaching the stage of non-retrogression; innumerable sentient beings received the prediction of their future enlightenment. The Immaculate World shook in six ways, and in the Sahā World, three thousand sentient beings dwelt on the stage of non-retrogression, while another three thousand sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and received their predictions. Thus, there were four groups who benefited.
In the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits," there are eleven stages of attaining realization and one stage of generating the resolve for enlightenment.

When the Buddha spoke of the long duration of the Tathāgata’s lifespan, six hundred and eighty trillion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); one thousand billion Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas attained the *dhāraṇī* gate of hearing and retaining;
and furthermore, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas equal in number to the atoms within a world-system attained the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*). One world...
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a world-system attained the immeasurable *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī* (revolving dhāraṇī) of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions;
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a trichiliocosm were able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma;
and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in two thousand lands were able to turn the pure Dharma.
Regarding the wheel, there are Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas equal in number to the atoms of a small thousandfold world-system who shall attain [enlightenment] after eight births;

those equal in number to the atoms of four sets of four-continent worlds who shall attain it after four births; those equal in number to the atoms of three sets of four-continent worlds who shall attain it after three births;

those equal in number to the atoms of two sets of four-continent worlds who shall attain it after two births; and Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas equal in number to the atoms of one set of four-continent worlds who shall attain it after one birth.
He shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
furthermore, sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds will all resolve their minds toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
As it is said in the "Chapter on the Medicine King," eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas attained the dhāraṇī for understanding the languages of all sentient beings.

When the "Chapter on the Wonderful Sound" was preached, eighty-four thousand people attained the samādhi of manifesting all physical forms, forty-two thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue attained the Lotus Samādhi.

When the "Avalokiteśvara Chapter" was preached, eighty-four thousand sentient beings all resolved to attain the peerless, unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
When the "Dhāraṇī Chapter" was preached, sixty-eight thousand people attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When the "Chapter on the Past Deeds of King Subhavyūha" was preached, eighty-four thousand people were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

When the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Exhortation" was preached, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the *śata-sahasra-āvarta-dhāraṇī*, and bodhisattvas equal in number to the atoms within a trichiliocosm practiced the path of Samantabhadra.

The five previous predictions recorded that they would attain Buddhahood; these twenty-five classes [of beings] are currently realizing the causal stage, and thus all benefit the present. Therefore, regarding those who benefit the future after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—the merit obtained through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* after the assembly has dispersed—all such constitutes benefiting the future.

The "Chapter on Rejoicing in Merit" describes the merit of the fiftieth person who, upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, is able to rejoice; this merit exceeds that of giving gold, silver, and the seven treasures to sentient beings throughout four million *nayuta* of trichiliocosm worlds, and it is also superior to causing them to attain the fruit of Arhatship.

If one goes to a monastic dwelling for even a brief moment to listen to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, in every successive birth they shall always ride upon elephants, horses, chariots, and palanquins made of the seven treasures, as well as celestial palaces.
Furthermore, if one shares their seat with others to enable them to listen, in every successive birth they shall always obtain the seat of Śakra or the seat of Brahmā.

Moreover, if one encourages others to go and listen to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, in every successive birth they shall always be born in the same place as dhāraṇī-holding bodhisattvas and shall never be mute; furthermore, they shall eventually behold the Buddhas of the future, hear the Dharma, and faithfully accept its instructions.

The "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master" states: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this Lotus Sūtra, that person shall obtain eight hundred merits of the eye, twelve hundred merits of the ear, eight hundred merits of the nose, twelve hundred merits of the tongue, eight hundred merits of the body, and twelve hundred merits of the mind. Adorned by these merits, their six sense faculties shall all be made pure."
Furthermore, the "Universal Worthy Chapter" states:

"If there are those in future generations who uphold, receive, read, and recite this sutra, such persons shall no longer be greedily attached to clothing, bedding, food and drink, or the necessities of life; their aspirations shall not be in vain, and they shall also obtain their rewards of merit in the present life."
Therefore, the *Śālistamba Sūtra* (The Sūtra of the Bequeathed Teaching) states:
"Those who were to be delivered have all been delivered; as for those not yet delivered, the causes and conditions for their deliverance have also already been established."
Therefore, by speaking this, great benefit is brought about for the future; this is called "benefiting those who come later," which is why this sutra is preached.
Within the manifestation of the timing, there are two aspects:
first, manifesting the time; second, manifesting the capacity [of the audience].
Regarding the initial manifestation [of the teaching], the Buddhas’ establishment of the doctrine is briefly of two kinds:
first, the sudden (tun), and second, the gradual (jian).

The sudden is intended for those of great capacity, who seek the fruit of Buddhahood directly from the state of an ordinary person; this is as described in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* regarding the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), where the One Vehicle is provisional and the Four Vehicles are real.
This [teaching] gradually accords with those whose capacities range from small to great; as explained in this sutra, the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is the reality because the Two Vehicles are provisional.
This sutra primarily accords with those who seek the fruit of Buddhahood by means of the Two Vehicles, and for the most part, it is subsumed within the gradual teaching of the Mahāyāna.
There is an ancient explanation stating that the teaching has five periods. As for the first period:

when the Buddha had first attained enlightenment, he taught the three refuges, the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, and the worldly causes and effects for the sake of Trapusa and Bhallika and five hundred merchants. This refers to the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Fundamental Practice of the Five Precepts) and similar texts; at that time, there were no yet beings with the capacity for supramundane roots of goodness.

As for the second period: after the Buddha had completed his enlightenment and passed the twenty-one days, for twelve years he taught only the doctrines of the three vehicles with practice, but had not yet taught emptiness; these are the Hinayana sutras such as the *Āgamas*.

Regarding the third period: during the thirty years following the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment, he taught the doctrine of emptiness common to the three vehicles; these include such works as the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Saṃghāṭa*, and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*.

Regarding the fourth period: during the forty years following the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment, he taught that there is a single vehicle (*ekayāna*), yet he had not yet clearly expounded the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the eternally abiding Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*). He still taught the impermanent state of Buddhahood as being the ultimate truth; this refers to such sutras as the *Anantamukha-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. This is because the meaning of the single vehicle had not been clarified previously, and within these [teachings], the eternally abiding Buddha-nature had likewise not yet been clearly expounded.

The fifth period refers to the teaching within the Śāla Grove that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature which is eternally abiding; this includes such scriptures as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Mahākaruṇā Sūtra*.

At first glance, this may seem plausible, yet in principle it is not so. The *Tiwai jing* (Sutra of Tiwei) states that five hundred merchants, prior to receiving the five precepts, first repented of their five heinous crimes, ten evil deeds, and offenses such as slandering the Dharma. They attained the fundamental purity of the four great elements, the fundamental purity of the five aggregates (*skandhas*), the fundamental purity of the six sense objects (*dhātus*), and the fundamental purity of the self. At that time, Tiwei and his companions attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); three hundred merchants attained the patience of compliance (*anuloma-kṣānti*); two hundred merchants attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*); the four heavenly kings and others attained the patience of compliance; three hundred dragon kings attained the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*); all other devas and the like resolved upon the unsurpassed path; and one billion devas and humans all practiced the ten wholesome paths of a bodhisattva.

The elder Trapusa extinguished the suffering of the three realms and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which corresponds to either the first bhūmi or the eighth bhūmi.

Furthermore, in the second week [after his enlightenment], as recorded in the *Lalitavistara-sūtra*, Trapusa and five hundred merchants offered the Buddha parched grain and honey; the Buddha then bestowed upon them this prediction:
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Samantagupta."
Why is it said that this first [teaching] is merely a worldly instruction?

It is because on this day, the truth (*satya*) observed equally by those of the three vehicles was not yet clearly explained; therefore, it was not yet called the "Turning of the Wheel of Dharma. It was only upon reaching the time of the five bhikṣus that it was designated as the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
Regarding the second period of twelve years during which only the provisional teachings were expounded, Jue’ai says:
In the fifth year after his enlightenment, he preached the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, which primarily elucidates the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);

furthermore, in the seventh year, for the sake of the eight bodhisattvas, he preached the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*, which primarily elucidates that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of sentient beings are fundamentally empty.

Furthermore, in the ninth year he preached the *Aṅgulimāla-samādhi-sūtra*, and in the tenth year he preached the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*; both clarify the profound principle of nirvāṇa and buddha-nature.

Furthermore, both the *Tiwai jing* and the *Puyao jing* clarify the practices of a bodhisattva; moreover, they record the bestowal of predictions for attaining Buddhahood upon merchants, demonstrating that the Mahāyāna was taught immediately after his initial attainment of the Way.
Furthermore, having completed his realization of the Way, on the second seven-day period he preached the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*. Moreover, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"When the Buddha was at Deer Park turning the wheel of the Four Noble Truths, immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon the state of a Śrāvaka; immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon the state of a Pratyekabuddha; immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and practiced the six pāramitās; immeasurable Bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and dwelt in the first, second, third, and even the tenth bhūmis; and immeasurable Bodhisattvas in their final birth before Buddhahood (*eka-jāti-pratibaddha*) simultaneously attained Buddhahood."
How can it be said that during the second period, he taught only the doctrines of the three vehicles?

This shows that while a single rain universally moistens all, the understanding received by various beings differs; thus, one cannot say that the Buddha’s teachings necessarily possess a sequence of priority and posteriority.

Now, relying on the ancient interpretation, I shall first refute the two time-periods; the remaining three time-periods will likewise be refuted as the ancients did. Although this approach may seem acceptable at first glance, it is logically untenable. Fearing that the text would become overly prolix, I shall briefly conclude here.

According to the newly translated sutras, the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna consists of only a single period; it does not arise from a lesser capacity but is directed toward a single type of faculty. Since the teaching is intended for only one [type of] recipient, the gradual Mahāyāna teaching, by contrast, possesses three periods.

The Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata, having attained profound understanding, extensively explained the various analogies of worldly viśvabheṣaja medicine, writing with multicolored threads upon the ground, clarified butter, and space; thereupon, the World-Honored One praised him for his excellent comprehension of what was taught.
Paramārthasamudgata addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In the beginning, at one time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana. There, solely for those setting out on the Śrāvaka Vehicle, he turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma by means of the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths. Although this was most wonderful and extremely rare, such that no one in any world could turn it, the wheel of Dharma turned at that time was surpassable and subject to further qualification; it was of provisional meaning and served as a basis for various disputes."

In the past, during the second turning of the wheel, the Blessed One, solely for those who had set out to practice the Mahāyāna, turned the wheel of the true Dharma by means of the hidden aspect—that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, are without arising or ceasing, and are from the beginning quiescent and by nature in nirvāṇa. Although this was even more marvelous and exceedingly rare, [it remains surpassed].

Furthermore, the wheel of Dharma turned at that time was also characterized by acceptance [of diverse views], was not yet of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and served as a basis for various disputes.

Now, during this third period, the World-Honored One, for the sake of those who have set out upon all vehicles, has turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma by means of the characteristic of clear manifestation—based on the fact that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, are without arising or ceasing, are primordially quiescent, and are by nature in nirvāṇa through the very absence of intrinsic nature. This is most marvelous and most rare.
Now, the Wheel of Dharma turned by the World-Honored One is unsurpassed and admits of no further inclusion; it is the definitive meaning, not a place where various disputes can find footing.

Based on this scriptural passage, the *Āgama* sūtras and others constitute the first period, in which existence is taught in a general and implicit manner, without clarifying what the nature of that existence is.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and other such sutras constitute the second period, which provides a general, implicit teaching on emptiness, without clarifying that those who do not understand emptiness are also empty of intrinsic nature.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and others constitute the third period, which explicitly teaches existence—namely, the dependent and the perfected natures—and also explicitly teaches emptiness as the emptiness of the imagined nature.
Therefore, the *Śīla-sūtra* and other texts state:
"The conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are called 'existence' (*sat*), while 'self' (*ātman*) and 'what belongs to the self' (*ātmīya*) are called 'emptiness' (*śūnya*).
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* also speaks of three wheels of Dharma, namely: the wheel of turning (*pravartana*), the wheel of illumination (*prabhāsana*), and the wheel of maintenance (*dhāraṇa*).
The Dharma of the Four Truths is turned so that one may illuminate existence through emptiness, for it is by being neither existent nor empty that it can be sustained.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also says:

Subsequently, when the king fell ill, he inquired about the appropriate medicine.
The physician again prepared a medicinal prescription, mixing the medicine with milk.
The king, filled with anger, questioned him:

This sutra is intended for those of the fixed nature of the Mahāyāna, the fixed nature of the Śrāvaka, and the indeterminate nature, as previously cited; however, there is no textual passage specifically addressing the capacity of the Pratyekabuddha. Second, I shall clarify the fundamental purport of the sutra. The virtuous masters of this land have generally categorized the sutras and śāstras into four schools:

first, the School of Establishing Nature (*Lixing zong*), such as the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* and others, because they establish that the five aggregates of phenomena possess intrinsic nature.
Second is the school that refutes substantiality (*svabhāva*), which is the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*; it refutes the existence of a substance in phenomena, asserting that there is only their appearance.
Third is the school that refutes characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), which includes the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and others; it refutes the characteristics of phenomena, establishing them as empty.
The fourth is the school that reveals the ultimate reality, such as the *Nirvāṇa*, *Avataṃsaka*, and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras, because they reveal the meaning of the true Middle Way.
This sutra represents the fourth school of tenets.
Furthermore, the fundamental tenets of ancient scriptures and treatises are extremely numerous: the four old *Āgamas* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* represent the doctrines of the Mahāsāṃghika school;
the *Sammitīya-śāstra* represents the doctrines of the Sthavira school.
The *Śāriputrābhidharma* and the *Brahmajāla-ṣaṣṭidṛṣṭi-sūtra* represent the tenets of the Saṃmitīya school;
the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* represents the tenets of the Dharmaguptaka school.
To which schools do these sūtras and śāstras belong?

However, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* and the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra-śāstra* state that there are twenty Hinayāna schools: namely, the Mahāsāṃghika, Ekavyāvahārika, Lokottaravāda, Kaukkuṭika, Bahuśrutīya, Prajñaptivāda, Caitika, Aparaśaila, Uttaraśaila, Sarvāstivāda, Sannagarika, Vātsīputrīya, Dharmottarīya, Bhadrayānīya, Saṃmitīya, Rājagirika, Mahīśāsaka, Dharmaguptaka, Kāśyapīya, and Sautrāntika;
together with two Mahāyāna schools, they constitute twenty-two sects.
Now, judging the teachings according to the texts, there are only three;
yet if one infers the tenets by analogy, there are eight.
As for the three teachings:

First, the school that predominantly asserts existence: this refers to the doctrines of the various *Āgamas* and other Śrāvaka vehicles; although they predominantly assert existence, they do not contradict emptiness.

Second, the school that predominantly asserts emptiness: this refers to the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Śata-śāstra*, the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtras*, and so forth; although they predominantly assert emptiness, they do not contradict existence.

The third is the school that is neither [purely] empty nor [purely] existent; this includes the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and others. These teach that conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena are designated as "existent," while the self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) are designated as "empty. Regarding these three teachings, they are as cited in the preceding text.
There are eight schools of tenets:
first, those who maintain that both the self and phenomena exist, such as the Vātsīputrīyas;
second, those who maintain that phenomena exist while the self does not, such as the Sarvāstivādins.
1. The three dharmas have no coming or going (the Mahāsāṃghika school, etc.).
2. The four [kinds of] supernormal powers are both provisional and real (the Prajñaptivāda school, etc.).
3. The conventional is false while the ultimate is real (the Lokottaravāda school, etc.).
Sixth, all phenomena are merely names, as taught in works such as the *Ekottarika-āgama*.
Seventh, the ultimate truth is entirely empty; this is taught in sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and in treatises such as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and *Śata-śāstra* by Nāgārjuna and others.
The eighth is "Rational, Perfect, and Ultimate"; this refers to the path taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other such texts, as well as in the expositions of Asaṅga and others.

The doctrine of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* represents the school of the Sautrāntikas; it corresponds to the fourth category, "Provisional and Real through Manifestation. Although these distinctions amount to twenty-two categories in total, in terms of fundamental principles, no difference exceeds these eight.
However, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgata expounds an ocean of boundless sūtras within a single utterance.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* says:
“The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single sound, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind.
The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* states:

“Since I attained the Way more than forty years ago, I have constantly taught that all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished, neither departing nor arriving, without this or that, without gain or loss, and entirely without marks; yet it is only because sentient beings differ in their realization and understanding that they obtain various different fruits.”
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also says:
"A single rain universally moistens all, yet the three types of grasses and two types of trees grow differently.
The *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* says:
"The three animals crossing the river distinguish between shallow and deep.

Thus we know that all teachings are fundamentally without distinction; it is only because of differences in the capacities of sentient beings that the teachings of Great and Small, and Sudden and Gradual, were differentiated.

This sutra, for its part, belongs to the teaching of the Great Vehicle’s gradual approach. It is called "gradual" because it relies on the conversion and guidance of śrāvakas to lead them toward the Great Vehicle.

In the "Chapter on the Former Deeds of King Subhavyūha," eighty-four thousand people were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye; this refers to those who attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and so forth.

In the "Universal Gate Chapter," eighty-four thousand sentient beings all resolved their minds toward the peerless *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; thus, it may be considered the Sudden Teaching.

Thus we know that there is no distinction between the sudden and gradual teachings as separate doctrinal gates; they are differentiated according to the capacities of sentient beings, and therefore these [teachings] are mutually inclusive. The two teachings of the "Half" and the "Full" are both subsumed within the Full Vehicle (Pūrṇa-yāna).

The two types of emptiness—emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)—are encompassed by both teachings. Both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) can be integrated across the two gateways. The conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*) are divided into two according to their respective applications.
Although the general purport and fundamental principles are thus understood, the specific teaching elucidated here takes the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) as its primary tenet.
Therefore, the text below states:

"In this present sutra, only the One Vehicle is taught; whereas previously, before the bodhisattvas, the Buddha disparaged the śrāvakas who delight in inferior teachings, yet in reality, the Buddha has always taught through the Mahāyāna. Regarding the third point, the derivation of the title of this scripture: as for the title *Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra*, in the Sanskrit it is called *saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Here, *sat* carries the meaning of "correct" or "wondrous."

"Puṇḍarīka" refers to the white lotus.

“Lotus” (*padma*) refers to the fruit of the *fúqú* (water lily); “flower” (*puṣpa*) refers to the blossom, as that which is beautiful in its blossoming is called a flower.
“Sūtra” (*sūtrānta*) means a discourse.
In terms of meaning, it should be called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

This is why it is said below that he emits white light from his ūrṇā-kośa and is drawn by white oxen; for white is the fundamental basis upon which all colors depend, and the One Vehicle is likewise the source of all vehicles.
